uses: Lemon balm is traditionally brewed as a gentle tea to settle the nerves, lift low spirits and help with sleep, and to ease bloating and wind. Old writers praised it for gladdening the heart and sharpening the memory. A hot cup was a household standby for feverish colds. Its leaves flavored cordials, balm wine and summer drinks, and it was the main herb in the old Carmelite water.
energetics: Culpeper called balm hot and dry
caution_pregnancy: Safety during pregnancy and breastfeeding has not been established. Not enough is known; avoid. The EMA does not recommend lemon balm medicines then.
caution_medications: The EMA found no data on interactions with medicines. Because lemon balm can make some people drowsy, check with a pharmacist before combining it with sleep aids, sedatives, alcohol or any other medicine.
caution_conditions: It may make you drowsy and affect your ability to drive or use machinery; don't drive if you feel affected. Medicinal use isn't established for children under 12. Avoid it if you are allergic to it.
caution_duration: The EMA advises seeing a practitioner if symptoms last longer than two weeks. None of our sources describes the safety of long-term use.
caution_topical: None of our sources gives a skin warning, but they cover use by mouth only, so not enough is known about skin use. Stop if irritation appears.
garden_harvest_timing: In the first year cut the top few inches when it flowers; established plants can be cut two or three times a season. Use fresh when you can, as dried leaves lose scent.
notes: Forms large clumps fast and can reseed hard; deadhead after flowering. Its small white flowers are rich in nectar and loved by bees. Not related to bee balm (Monarda). Grieve tells of beekeepers rubbing hives with the leaves to keep a swarm together.
